fixes.explanation: Right on the money, friend. The text says, “Behold, the Lord will impoverish her…” (Zechariah 9:4). Tyre had silver like dust and gold like the dirt of the streets. Then the Lord says He'll cast her wealth into the sea.

Tyre did build herself a fortress (Zechariah 9:3), so guarding walls is an easy guess. But the Lord doesn't say He'll guard them. He says she will be consumed by fire (Zechariah 9:4). The fortress is in verse 3, and what happens to her is in verse 4.

Yes, friend. Tyre built a fortress and heaped up silver and gold (Zechariah 9:3), but the verse says she will be consumed by fire (Zechariah 9:4). The text doesn't say the fortress keeps her safe. Fire is what's coming.

That's it. When Ashkelon sees what happens to Tyre, the text says, “Ashkelon will see and fear…” (Zechariah 9:5). Fear is the word for Ashkelon, not celebration. Gaza will writhe in agony, as will Ekron, in the same verse.
That's right, friend. The verse says, “There will cease to be a king in Gaza…” (Zechariah 9:5). Gaza is named right alongside Ashkelon and Ekron in that verse. Its king is part of what goes.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.” (Zechariah 9:6). A mixed race will occupy Ashdod. Then the verse names pride as the thing being cut off.

That's the surprise, friend. After the blood and the abominations are removed from their mouths, the text says, “Then they too will become a remnant for our God…” (Zechariah 9:7). The Philistines are described as God's remnant. That's quite a turn.
Yes! The text says the Philistines “…will become like a clan in Judah…” (Zechariah 9:7). They go from the burden list to being likened to a clan. And that clan is in Judah.
Egypt is a fair guess, since it's a big name in the Bible. But it isn't in this verse. The Philistines “…will become like a clan in Judah…” (Zechariah 9:7). Judah is the answer here.

That's the reason in the verse, baker. The LORD says, “…never again will an oppressor overrun My people, for now I keep watch with My own eyes.” (Zechariah 9:8). The promise rests on the LORD watching with His own eyes. The verse gives no other reason.

Walls feel like a natural reason, but the verse doesn't use it. Speaking of His people, the LORD says, “…for now I keep watch with My own eyes.” (Zechariah 9:8). Remember Tyre and her fortress, because this promise doesn't depend on walls.

That's right. The text says, “Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem!” (Zechariah 9:9). The reason comes in the next line: “See, your King comes to you…” After all the burden talk, this is a big change of mood.
Yes, baker. The text says, “…the bow of war will be broken.” (Zechariah 9:10). The chariot is cut off from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem. The bow goes with them.
Putting a bow in storage sounds tidy. The verse is stronger than that. It says, “…the bow of war will be broken.” (Zechariah 9:10). Broken is not the same as put away.
Yes! The text says, “Then He will proclaim peace to the nations.” (Zechariah 9:10). The chariot is cut off and the bow of war is broken. Then the King's message is peace.

War is a fair guess when chariots and bows are in the verse. But they're being cut off and broken, and then He proclaims something else. The text says, “Then He will proclaim peace to the nations.” (Zechariah 9:10). Peace is the word.

It sounds like a King would stay close to Jerusalem. But the verse goes far past that. It says, “His dominion will extend from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.” (Zechariah 9:10).

That's right. The text says, “His dominion will extend from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.” (Zechariah 9:10). It doesn't stop at Jerusalem. It reaches to the ends of the earth.

That's it, baker. Then the LORD speaks: “As for you, because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit.” (Zechariah 9:11). The prisoners are in a waterless pit. Because of the blood of His covenant, they are released.

A waterless pit sounds like a place with no way out. But the verse promises the opposite. The LORD says, “…because of the blood of My covenant, I will release your prisoners from the waterless pit.” (Zechariah 9:11). Release is the promise.

That's right. The LORD says, “Return to your stronghold, O prisoners of hope…” (Zechariah 9:12). The prisoners are released in verse 11, and the next verse gives them a direction. They aren't just released, they're told where to go.
Yes, baker. The LORD is speaking, and He says, “…I will rouse your sons, O Zion, against the sons of Greece.” (Zechariah 9:13). He has just said He will bend Judah as His bow.

You got it, friend. The LORD says, “…I will make you like the sword of a mighty man.” (Zechariah 9:13). Earlier in the verse He says He will bend Judah as His bow. So Judah is as a bow, and Zion will be like a sword.
A wall of bronze would be solid, no question. But the verse picks a weapon, not a wall. The LORD says, “…I will make you like the sword of a mighty man.” (Zechariah 9:13). It's a sword.

A lion is a strong picture, and I see why you went there. But it isn't the one in this verse. The LORD says, “…I will make you like the sword of a mighty man.” (Zechariah 9:13). The picture here is a sword.
That's right! The text says, “Then the LORD will appear over them, and His arrow will go forth like lightning.” (Zechariah 9:14). The LORD appears over them. His arrow is likened to lightning.

Yes, baker. The text says, “The LORD of Hosts will shield them.” (Zechariah 9:15). The ram's horn is in the verse right before it (Zechariah 9:14). In verse 15, the LORD of Hosts is the one who shields.

Returning comes up earlier in the chapter, when the prisoners are told to return to their stronghold (Zechariah 9:12). But this verse is about the battle. The text says, “The LORD of Hosts will shield them.” (Zechariah 9:15). The word here is shield.

That's right. The text says, “…they will be filled like sprinkling bowls, drenched like the corners of the altar.” (Zechariah 9:15). The people are likened to bowls that are full. And they're drenched like the corners of the altar.

Sparkling right, baker! The text says, “…like jewels in a crown they will sparkle over His land.” (Zechariah 9:16). Jewels are the picture of how His people will shine. The verse says the LORD their God will save them as the flock of His people.
Feathers might look nice on a crown, but that's not what this verse says. The text says, “…like jewels in a crown they will sparkle over His land.” (Zechariah 9:16). Jewels are what sparkle.

After a battle you'd expect a tired bunch. But the chapter ends somewhere else. The last verse says, “How lovely they will be, and how beautiful! Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine, the young women.” (Zechariah 9:17). The people are lovely and beautiful there, and the young men and women flourish.

Yes, friend. The last verse says, “How lovely they will be, and how beautiful! Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine, the young women.” (Zechariah 9:17). They end up lovely and beautiful. The young men and women flourish, and the chapter closes on that.
